quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

No statewide civil death registration until 1913 — probate/estate files (1753-1970) are the primary substitute. collections.title: Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (synthetic test fixture)

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: Tree fact F2 records Patrick's death 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County (source S3, PA death certificate). Tree states birth ~1845 in Ireland, while the objective says Pennsylvania; this item helps settle that.

That is co-residence only and does not prove parentage. The 1860 and 1870 schedules show household members and neighbors; 1880 is the first census recording relationship to head, useful for siblings and any later household of Patrick.

Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records is name-searchable. Search Flynn baptisms, marriages and burials for Patrick, variants Flin, Flinn, Flyn, Floyd. loc_001: Catholic registers sit with parish/Archdiocese of Philadelphia, so a missing index hit may require the parish itself. A baptism may not exist: Patrick appears to be born ca. 1845 in Ireland per the tree, before any Schuylkill register, so this also targets his own burial entry (item 4) and his marriage.

Patrick's own burial entry after his 1908-03-12 death: cemetery and parish burial registers, interment records and obituary notices often state age, birthplace and relatives, and identify adjacent family plots (possibly Thomas Flynn). Used because the baptism likely does not exist (born Ireland ca. 1845 per tree).

Patrick's own marriage record (county marriages 1885-1950 and civil marriages 1677-1950 are name-searchable) may name his parents and shows where he married; his wife's record gives context for FAN identification.

entry.jurisdiction: Ireland and Schuylkill, Pennsylvania, United States
entry.rationale: Dedicated item for the candidate parents' marriage to each other: Thomas Flynn (tree: b. ~1818 Ireland, linked to Patrick only via the 1850 census) and a wife whose name is not yet known. It would confirm them as a couple, supply the wife's name (a later or earlier marriage is possible, so any surname found is not assumed to be her birth name) and its date relative to Patrick's ~1845 birth corroborates the link. items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

1882 city/county directory: Michael Sheahan, occupation 'miner', Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. Establishes the 'after' point. Neither record explains the move itself -- found incidentally, not part of any plan.

The United States Census, 1880 is name-searchable and falls between the two points: it shows whether he was already in the county, his occupation, household, birthplace, and whether he lived with or near brother Patrick (who bought land in Schuylkill in 1875). Search Sheahan/Sheehan/Shehan/Sheehan variants.

FAN item: the tree records Patrick Sheahan purchasing land from James Kelly in 1875 (Deed Book 42 p. 118, S1). Examine that deed and later Sheahan deeds/leases for Michael as grantee, witness, or neighbor, and for Kelly as a possible kin or employer link that drew the family to the county. loc_001 notes that coal-region land was often leased from mining companies, so Michael may appear in no deed; absence is informative. items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.notes: 1870 census: Michael Sheahan, farmer, household outside Schuylkill County. Establishes the 'before' point -- not yet in the coal region and not yet employed in mining.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

items.notes: Patrick Flynn age 15 in household of Thomas Flynn, Schuylkill Co. Consistent with 1850 placement.
Death certificate found. Names Thomas Flynn as father. Informant was son-in-law James Brown.

entry.rationale: Tree records Patrick (I1) b. ~1845 with father Thomas (I2) b. ~1818 Ireland, from the 1850 and 1860 censuses (1860: Patrick age 15 in Thomas's Schuylkill household) and the 1908 death certificate naming Thomas. Patrick would be ~25 in 1870, possibly still in or near Thomas's household or newly married. United States Census, 1870 is name-searchable. Search Flynn/Patrick with variants (Flinn, Flin, Flyn, Patt, Patk) and Thomas in Schuylkill and adjoining coal-region counties; 1870 gives no relationships, so infer from household order and neighbors. Note the question says born PA while the tree says Ireland: record stated birthplace.

United States Census, 1880 is name-searchable and is the first census stating relationship to head and each person's parents' birthplaces: it can show Patrick as head or as son in Thomas's household (Thomas ~62 if alive), and his own children, with parents' birthplaces confirming an Irish-born father. Search variant spellings; Patrick's household and neighbors (possible kin) also noted.

The 1890 census was destroyed by fire, so 1900 is the next survivor and bridges 1880 to the 1908 death. United States Census, 1900 is name-searchable and records birth month/year, years married, immigration year and parents' birthplaces; look for Patrick as head and any Thomas (would be ~82) in the household or as a widowed boarder. Use the 1908 death certificate informant (son-in-law James Brown) to check the household/neighbors.

Dedicated item for the candidate parents' marriage to each other (Thomas Flynn and a wife whose name is not yet known): confirms them as a couple, supplies the mother's maiden name that census and the death certificate omit, and by date relative to ~1845 corroborates Thomas as father. It does not alone prove Patrick is their child. loc_001: Catholic registers are held at the parish/diocese of Philadelphia, not county; pre-1906 there was no civil registration. Marriage may be in Ireland (tree places Thomas's birth there), so also consider Irish parish records. Census items 1-3 supply the wife's name first.

FAN/direct item: a will or administration for Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818, could die from 1860 to roughly 1900, sized to Thomas's lifespan not Patrick's) held by the Schuylkill County Register of Wills from 1811 (loc_001) would name heirs, including Patrick, plus witnesses, appraisers and bondsmen who are associates. Run after the censuses indicate when Thomas disappears.

Patrick's own burial entry (parish or cemetery register) after the 12 March 1908 death: the death certificate is already found (names Thomas as father), but a baptism may not exist because Patrick was possibly born in Ireland before parish registers; burial records may give age, birthplace and adjacent family plots, with Thomas possibly buried nearby.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

**Plan pl_003, in order (all FamilySearch):**
1. pli_006, census 1870, Schuylkill County. It is name-searchable and tracks Patrick at about 25. The schedule has no relationship column.
2. pli_007, census 1880. It is name-searchable and is the first census to give relationship to head, so Thomas as father or father-in-law would be direct evidence. It also gives parents' birthplaces.
3. pli_008, census 1900. It is name-searchable. The 1890 census was largely destroyed, so it cannot bridge the gap. This item covers the later part of the window.

7. pli_012, vital record. This is the FAN item, covering James Brown, Patrick's children and neighbors. Their records may name Thomas as grandfather or Patrick's parents.

No item is a fallback for another.

**Hand-back:** run search-records on pli_006, pli_007 and pli_008 first.

---

The question is who Patrick Flynn's parents were. Records so far show a Thomas Flynn as his father, but only the 1908 death certificate says so directly, and the 1850 and 1860 censuses only list them in one household. The new plan starts with the 1870, 1880 and 1900 censuses. It looks for Patrick as an adult and for Thomas living with him or Patrick listed as his son. The 1880 census is the most useful, because it is the first to state each person's relationship to the head of household. After the censuses, the plan looks for Thomas's will or estate papers. It then looks for the marriage of Thomas and Patrick's mother, Patrick's own marriage and burial entries, and records of his son-in-law and neighbors. These could each name his parents.

Next I'll search the 1870, 1880 and 1900 census indexes for Patrick and Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County, allowing for spelling variants.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: Tree records Patrick's death 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County (S3, Pennsylvania Death Certificates). Statewide registration began 1906 (loc_001), so this certificate exists. The collection Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968 is name-searchable. Read the image for parents' names, birthplace and informant (derivative information), and for the burial place that points to a church and cemetery. Note the tree and timeline say Ireland ~1845 while the question says PA; the certificate's birthplace tests that.

The 1850 census (searched, log_001/002) shows Patrick age 5 in Thomas Flynn's household, dwelling 84; that is co-residence only and does not prove parentage (ps_001). 1860 and 1870 are name-searchable and fill the 1851-1860 gap in the timeline; 1880 records relationship to head and parents' birthplaces. 1900 gives birth month/year and immigration year. Collections: United States Census 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900, all name-searchable. Search Patrick and Thomas households, noting siblings and a mother.

loc_001: Catholic registers are held by the parish/Archdiocese of Philadelphia, not the county. Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (name-searchable) may hold Patrick's baptism if he was born in PA, his marriage, his burial in 1908, and siblings' baptisms. Because the tree says he was born in Ireland, a baptism in this county may not exist, so the burial and marriage entries (age, origin parish) are the likely route. Try Flynn variants Flinn, Flin, Flyn.

Patrick's own marriage: church or civil marriage entries often name parents or an age and birthplace. Pennsylvania, County Marriages 1885-1950 and Civil Marriages 1677-1950 are name-searchable; counties did not register earlier marriages statewide, so church registers (item 3) cover earlier years. Also serves as a source for the spouse's family as FAN.

Dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818 Ireland, in tree as the candidate father from the 1850 census only) to Patrick's mother, whose name is unknown. It would confirm the couple as a unit, give the mother's maiden name only if this was her first marriage (a later remarriage is possible and no surname is assumed), and its date relative to ~1845 corroborates the father. It does not by itself prove Patrick is their son; that needs item 2, 3 or 6. Search Pennsylvania Civil Marriages and Compiled Marriages (name-searchable) and Schuylkill church registers; the marriage may predate arrival in the US, so an Irish parish marriage is possible.

Register of Wills holds wills and administrations from 1811 (loc_001). Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683-1994 is browse-only (personCount 0): browse images by county and surname, not a name search. Window is set by Thomas's lifespan (b. ~1818, could die to about 1900), so it extends beyond Patrick's 1908 death; also check Patrick's own estate (1908) for heirs and any mother or siblings named. Creditors, appraisers and bondsmen are FAN names.

FAN item: neighbors on the 1850 census pages near dwelling 84, other Flynn households in the same ward, and godparents or witnesses in the Flynn church entries. Coal-region Irish immigrants often traveled with kin and neighbors from the same parish; those households could state a shared origin or relationship to Thomas. Also siblings of Patrick (to be identified in items 2 and 3): their marriages and deaths often name parents.

Tree gives birth ~1845 in Ireland, which conflicts with the PA birth in the question. Naturalization declarations of Thomas Flynn (or Patrick) name the origin and arrival year. loc_001 notes coal-region naturalization films are browse-only image groups (record-searchable ~0%), so use volume_search to find them and browse images. Also check the Civil War Soldiers Index (name-searchable) for Patrick or a brother, as service records and pensions may name parents.

If items 1-8 show an Irish birth, the baptism is in an Irish parish register that is not name-indexed. Run a full-text co-occurrence search on Flynn plus the mother's name (once found), unscoped across the corpus, executed via search-full-text; this is a follow-on contingent on a parish being named, so do not run it until an origin is identified.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1838-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: Tree holds only Bridget Halloran (b. ~1838 Ireland) with spouse John Doyle and daughter Ellen Doyle; no other children, no dates. Log_002 (1900 census) shows Bridget bore 9 children, 2 living. Catholic baptisms name both parents, so they are the most direct evidence of siblings. 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' is name-searchable. loc_001: Catholic registers stay with the Philadelphia diocese/parish, so search by parents John Doyle and Bridget (Halloran/Holloran/Halleran variants; Doyle/Doyl/Dolan) with no child name, and note sponsors.

Dedicated search for the marriage of John Doyle and Bridget Halloran to each other (church register or civil). It confirms them as a couple and dates the union, which bounds when children could be born; Ellen's marriage entry (log_003) names them as parents but the union itself is undocumented. Marriage could be outside Schuylkill (Ireland or elsewhere), so also try the name-searchable Pennsylvania Civil Marriages and Compiled Marriages collections. It does not by itself prove children, which need items 1, 3-5. County Marriages 1885-1950 does not cover this period, so it is not used.

United States Census, 1860 is name-searchable. Should show John and Bridget Doyle with young children (Ellen plus siblings) before the death of John. Search household by parents' names and by Ellen with ages and Irish birthplaces; record neighbors (FAN).

United States Census, 1870 is name-searchable. Captures the household nearer the end of the Doyle marriage or a widowed Bridget with children, and catches children born 1860-1870. Also search Doyle children living with relatives or as boarders, since only 2 of 9 survived to 1900.

United States Census, 1880 is name-searchable and records relationship to head. Bridget remarried Martin Kearney in 1879 (log_001), so look for the Kearney household with Doyle children as stepchildren, plus any grown Doyle children elsewhere. Search under Kearney, Halloran and Doyle.

John Doyle's own death or burial entry (he died before the 1879 remarriage, log_001), in the church records and cemetery records. Burial entries can name widow and sometimes children; pre-1906 there is no civil death registration (loc_001). Establishes the cut-off for Doyle children and the death date to search probate and newspapers.

Register of Wills: administration or estate of John Doyle (letters naming widow and heirs, guardianship of minor children) and later estates of Martin Kearney and Bridget Kearney. Window is set by the creators' lifespans: John d. before 1879, Bridget (b. ~1838) could die as late as ~1920. Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683-1994 is browse-only (personCount 0), so browse the county docket images by name index instead of name search. loc_001 confirms the Register of Wills is the primary heir-naming source.

FAN and sibling records: marriages of Doyle children (Ellen's was found, log_003) whose entries name parents John Doyle and Bridget Halloran. Search marriages by that parent pairing in Pennsylvania County Marriages (name-searchable, from 1885) and in Civil and Compiled Marriages for earlier years. Each such entry identifies a sibling by direct parent naming.

Death certificates of Bridget Kearney and of Ellen and any surviving second child. Pennsylvania Death Certificates 1906-1968 is name-searchable; the 1900 census shows 2 children living, so the other survivor may be an informant or named in obituaries. Parent names on a child's certificate give John Doyle and Bridget as parents.

Anthracite-region newspapers: any mining-accident or death notice for John Doyle (children often named in coal-region accident reports) and obituaries of Bridget Kearney naming surviving children. Pre-1906 there is no civil death record (loc_001), so these cover deaths of the 7 unsurviving children too. Repository to be found via a newspaper index; not yet confirmed by tool.

## Stagstrup Sogn, Thisted Amt, Denmark - late 1700s

For a male subject born 1779, two record classes carry parentage. Church books (kirkeboeger) hold the baptism naming both parents. The military levy rolls (laegdsruller), kept from 1789, enroll every boy under his father's name from childhood - direct evidence of the father. Danish patronymics (Nielsen = son of Niels) point to the father's given name but not the specific man. The Stagstrup register is only ~3% indexed, so plan to browse images.

entry.rationale: Tree holds only Mikkel's birth, 20 Aug 1779 at Stagstrup, with no parents, relationships or sources. The baptism entry names both parents, so it is the most direct answer. loc_001: the Stagstrup register is only about 3% name-indexed, so browse register images (image group 004130616, covering 1763-1814) around Aug-Sep 1779 rather than relying on the index. Check variant spellings (Mikkel/Michel/Mikkell, Blyeberg/Blybjerg).

Per the fetched Denmark Military Records page and loc_001, levying rolls from 1788/1789 list every boy from birth under his father's name: direct parentage evidence independent of the baptism. Search the Denmark, Military Levying Rolls collection (2513529) by name, and browse volume 004748896 (0% record-searchable) if the search underdelivers, since place fields may rank rather than filter. Patronymic Nielsen implies father Niels, which does not identify which Niels, so match on the roll's household/number placement.

Dedicated item for the candidate parents' marriage to each other: a Niels and his wife marrying before 1779. It confirms the couple as a unit, gives the wife's name (maybe a patronymic, not a surname), and its date relative to 1779 corroborates the father. It does not by itself prove Mikkel is their child; the baptism or levy roll must place him with them. Browse register 004130616 (1763-1814); the marriage may fall in a neighbouring parish if the bride came from elsewhere.

FAN item: baptisms of siblings and the godparents (faddere) at Mikkel's baptism. Siblings' entries naming the same Niels and mother test the candidate couple, and sponsors are often kin. Browse register 004130616.

Burial of the candidate father Niels (to establish the death date the objective asks for), and of the mother. Window runs from the 1779 birth to the register end in 1814, as father could die at any point; burial entries give age and often farm/place. Browse register 004130616; later years need the Church Books collection (2078555).

Probate (skifteprotokoller, volume 004392710, Hassing Herred 1690-1850, 0% record-searchable so browse). The father's estate division would list heirs, naming Mikkel as a son. Window sized to the father's plausible death (up to about 60 years after 1779), not Mikkel's life. Confirm first that Stagstrup lies in Hassing Herred; also check the mother's estate and any guardian entries.

Mikkel's own marriage and death/burial entries; these often give age, birthplace and sometimes parents' names, and cross-check the 1779 birth. Use Denmark, Church Books (2078555); his parish after 1814 is unknown, so start with Stagstrup and neighbouring parishes and use the levy rolls' parish numbers to trace moves.

items.guide_markdown:
## Muhlenberg County, Kentucky — c. 1870-1890

Statewide death certificates begin 1911; no certificate can cover a death in the 1870s-1880s. County death registers (1804888) exist but the 1860s-1870s coverage is partial. For this era, **probate records are the primary death evidence**: administrator bonds name the widow or heir, estate settlements are dated, and register entries bracket the death within months. Muhlenberg County probate (1875188) survives well for the 1870s and is browse-only. Supplement with church burials, cemetery records, and census bracketing.

entry.rationale: Review pending FamilySearch hints on ZZWK-EL1 before searching — an attached hint may already answer the question.

Tree records only Birth 1814 Kentucky and Residence 1870 Muhlenberg County. loc_001: statewide death certificates begin 1 Jan 1911, so a death after 1870 at age 56+ most likely predates them; probate is the primary death evidence. Kentucky Probate Records, 1727-1990 is browse-only (personCount 0): browse Muhlenberg County will books, administrator bonds, inventories and settlements, which bracket the death within months and place it in the county. Window runs to 1911 since he could have died up to age 97 and estates may be settled years later.

loc_001: Kentucky, Deaths and Burials, 1843-1970 holds county death registers for 1852-1910 with partial 1860s-1870s coverage; name-search for Elijah Wilkins (variants Wilkin, Wilkens, Wilkerson) in Muhlenberg and adjoining counties. A hit gives a date and place directly; a miss may reflect a lost register.

The question presupposes death certificates. loc_001 shows they start 1911, so this tests the premise: search Kentucky Deaths, 1911-1967 (name-searchable) for an Elijah Wilkins born c. 1814 to rule a late death in or out. A match at age 97+ needs strong identity checks; expected result is no match, confirming a pre-1911 death.

The 1870 residence is the last-known-alive anchor. Search the 1880 census (relationship to head, age, household) for Elijah and the 1900 census for any survivor; the first census without him, with a widow or mortality-schedule entry, brackets the death window. 1880 mortality schedule (deaths June 1879-May 1880) is included where available.

loc_001 notes church burial registers and cemetery records can bracket the death. Search Muhlenberg church burial registers and cemetery listings/Find a Grave for Elijah Wilkins; stones and burials give date and place and may name spouse and children, supporting identity.

Obituaries and death notices in Muhlenberg-area newspapers (e.g. via Chronicling America or Kentucky digital newspaper collections) may state the death date, place, age and survivors, corroborating probate dates and identity.

FAN item: the widow, adult sons or neighbours found in the 1870 household and as administrators or bondsmen in probate. Their own death certificates (1911+), probate, or marriage records may name Elijah Wilkins as father or give his death, and distinguish him from other Elijah Wilkinses in the county. Depends on names from items 2 and 5.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

entry.rationale: Review pending FamilySearch hints on ZZKR-BR1 before searching — an attached hint may already answer the question. The project tree records only a 1871 Pottsville birth for her and no baptism or sources.

Target record. The 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' collection is name-searchable. Search Bridget Kerrigan with variants (Kerrigan, Kerrican, Carrigan, Kerigan; Bridgit, Brigid, Delia/Bridie) and parents Thomas Kerrigan and Ellen Burke (Bourke, Burk). Irish Catholic families in Pottsville were under the Diocese of Philadelphia (loc_001); registers are held by parishes, and Latin entries may anglicize names. Civil birth registration began only in 1906, so a church register is the main source. Baptism usually followed birth within days or weeks, so the window runs to 1873.

Fallback if the name search fails: browse the church-records image group 007936751, which is browse-only (personCount 0). loc_001 notes coal-region church films are often unindexed. Browse the Pottsville Catholic parish baptism volumes for 1871-1872 image by image, and check for Latin entries and spelling variants.

FAN and sibling item. Search baptisms of other children of Thomas Kerrigan and Ellen Burke, and the sponsors (godparents) named in them. Siblings' entries show which Pottsville parish the family used, which tells us which register to browse for Bridget, and sponsors are kin or neighbours who may appear in hers. Also covers the parents' marriage (c. 1865-1870, Ellen was born in Ireland in 1846), which shows the family's parish. The marriage proves only their union, not Bridget's baptism.

Indirect: Bridget's own death certificate (if she died after 1906) may give a birth date and parents' names, which help match a baptism entry. The 'Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968' collection is name-searchable. Her death date and place are unknown, so search statewide.

Bridget's own marriage entry may give her age and birthplace or parents, which cross-check a baptism. Planned collections are 'Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950' (name-searchable) and the browse-only Schuylkill marriage volume 007936753 (personCount 0, 1870-1910). Her marriage may fall in or near Schuylkill; her spouse is unknown.

Church burial or cemetery records, and obituaries or parish records for Bridget, may give an age or birth date and her parish. Her father Thomas Kerrigan died by 1898 in Pottsville; his burial and obituary may name his parish and family. Check Find a Grave, Pottsville newspapers and parish cemetery registers.
